Exercise 4 — Aggregated Data and Global Spatial Autocorrelation

BSTA 374 · 17.5 points · Due Wednesday, October 14, 2026, 11:59 pm

Author

Abby Winters · Lehigh University

Published

October 14, 2026

What this exercise is

Exercises 1–3 ran on data that shipped inside an R package. This one does not. You will work with real surveillance data — COVID-19 deaths in the 67 counties of Pennsylvania — and assemble the analysis dataset yourself, the way you would in a health department: a table of counts from one source, county boundaries from another, and a join between them that has to be checked rather than trusted.

From there the exercise follows the sequence of the last two weeks:

  1. join and project the data;
  2. compute crude rates, expected counts, and the standardized mortality ratio (SMR);
  3. map the SMR honestly — which, for a ratio, is not the same as mapping a rate;
  4. build a spatial weights matrix and ask, with global Moran’s I, whether the SMRs are spatially structured or could plausibly be arranged at random.

It is worth 17.5 points and carries more weight than the first two exercises. Start early: Part A is where most of the unexpected problems will be.

WarningReproducibility is graded

Restart R and render from a clean session before you submit. The CSV must be in your repository (put it in a data/ folder) and be read with a relative path — read_csv("data/..."), never C:/Users/... — or the document will not render on my machine.

The data

Counts. pa_covid_deaths_2020.csv is posted on Course Site. It is a subset of the Johns Hopkins University CSSE COVID-19 Data Repository (time_series_covid19_deaths_US.csv), the source behind the JHU dashboard that was the most widely used COVID-19 tracker in the United States until the project stopped updating in March 2023. The repository compiles counts reported by state health departments — here, the Pennsylvania Department of Health — and attributes deaths to the county of residence.

Column Meaning
UID, FIPS JHU identifier; county FIPS code
Admin2 County name
Province_State State
Population County population (U.S. Census Bureau 2019 estimate, as carried in the JHU file)
deaths_2020 Cumulative COVID-19 deaths reported through December 31, 2020

Cite the source in your document as: Dong, E., Du, H., & Gardner, L. (2020). An interactive web-based dashboard to track COVID-19 in real time. The Lancet Infectious Diseases, 20(5), 533–534, together with the repository URL: https://github.com/CSSEGISandData/COVID-19.

Boundaries. County polygons come from the U.S. Census Bureau’s cartographic boundary files, downloaded inside your document with the tigris package. Install it once, in the console — install.packages(c("tigris", "ggrepel")) — not inside the document.

NoteWhy 2020

Calendar year 2020 is the first pandemic year and the period before vaccines were available. Treat the population as the population at risk for one year.

library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(leaflet)
library(spdep)
library(ggrepel)            # non-overlapping labels
library(tigris)
options(tigris_use_cache = TRUE)   # download once, then reuse

covid <- read_csv("pa_covid_deaths_2020.csv")
pa    <- counties(state = "PA", cb = TRUE, year = 2020)

Part A — Assemble the dataset (3 points)

  1. Inspect both objects. How many rows does covid have, and how many polygons does pa have? The two numbers differ. Find the rows responsible and say in one sentence what they are and why they cannot be mapped.

    Covid has 69 rows, while pa contains 67 polygons. The two extra rows that covid has which are “out of PA” and “unassigned” do not represent actual PA counties and cannot be mapped to county polygons.

  2. Identify the column in each object that identifies a county. Show what the values look like in each, and say why they will not match as they stand.

    The county identifier for covid is FIPS and for pa is GEOID. The values represent the same county codes but FIPS is stored as a numeric value and GEOID is stored as a character variable. They need to be converted to the same format before they can be matched.

  3. Create a join key in covid that matches the one in pa, then join the counts onto the polygons. Show, with code, that every one of the 67 counties received a count — do not just look at the map.

  4. In two or three sentences: why join the table onto the polygons (left_join(pa, covid)) rather than the other way around, and what would an inner join have hidden from you if the key had been only partly wrong?

The left code method that was used preserves all 67 county polygons, even if some counties fail to match during the join. This makes sure that we would be able to easily identify any join problems because unmatched counties will pop up with NA values. Using the inner method would remove unmatched counties completely and could hide these errors within the join key from us to see.

Tip

Run the obvious join first, left_join(pa, covid, by = c("GEOID" = "FIPS")), and read the error message carefully. It tells you exactly what is wrong. A FIPS code is an identifier, not a number: 42001 and 42001.0 are the same number but not the same identifier, and a county such as 01001 in Alabama would lose its leading zero.

Part B — Coordinate reference system (1.5 points)

  1. What CRS do the Census boundaries arrive in? Geographic or projected?

The Censis boundaries arrive in a geographic CRS. The output below tells us that the data is stored as longitude and latitude rather than projected coordinates.

  1. Transform pa_covid to a projected CRS appropriate for the whole state, and state its EPSG code. Pennsylvania is split between two State Plane zones (North and South) and two UTM zones, so the obvious choices each cover only part of the state — say what you chose and why it is acceptable for a statewide map.

    I chose the EPSG code to 5070 because it covers all the lower 48 states in a single coordinate system. Since PA spans multiple state plane and UTM zones, I chose this because it avoids splitting the state across zones while maintaining consistent spatial properties across the entire state.

  2. One sentence: which of the operations in this exercise actually depend on the projection, and which do not?

    Creating join keys joining covid data to polygons do not depend on the projection, but any calculations involving location, distance, area, or spatial analysis would need a projected CRS.

Starting code

st_crs(pa_covid)$input
[1] "NAD83"
st_is_longlat(pa_covid)
[1] TRUE
pa_covid <- st_transform(pa_covid, 5070)
st_is_longlat(pa_covid)
[1] FALSE

Part C — Counts, rates, expected counts, and the SMR (4.5 points)

  1. Compute the crude COVID-19 mortality rate per 100,000 for 2020 in every county. Report the three highest and three lowest.

    The three highest are Mifflin County with 257.9 deaths per 100,000, Northumberland County 248.8 deaths per 100,000, and Bedford County with 196.3 deaths per 100,000. The three lowest are Wayne County with 35 deaths per 100,000, Forest County with 41.4 deaths per 100,000, and Greene County with 41.4 deaths per 100,000.

  2. Make two quick static maps with ggplot2, placed side by side: the number of deaths as proportional symbols, and the crude rate as a choropleth with a sequential, colour-blind-safe palette. Both need a legend title with units. In two or three sentences: why is a count shown with symbols rather than a choropleth, which counties stand out on each map, and why do the two maps tell different stories?

    Death counts are shown with proportional symbols rather than a choropleth because counts are strongly influenced by county size and population and this makes large counties seem more important just because they have more people. On the deaths map, the largest points are around the most populated counties in eastern and southeastern PA, whereas the crude rate map highlights counties such as Mifflin, Northumberland, and Bedford since they had the highest mortality rates per 100,000 people. The two maps tell different stories because the symbol map shows just the total number of deaths, but the choropleth map shows the risk of death relative to the population size.

  3. Compute the statewide reference rate \(r = \sum_i O_i / \sum_i P_i\), and from it the expected count in each county, \(E_i = r \times P_i\). Show that \(\sum_i E_i = \sum_i O_i\) and explain in one sentence why this must be so.

    The statewide reference rate was 125.2149 deaths per 100,000 people and the total deaths across all counties was 16,030. This is equal to the total observed deaths, also 16,030. This must be true since the expected counts were calculated using the statewide rate so the statewide total has to be preserved when the rate is applied to each county population.

  4. Compute the SMR, \(O_i / E_i\).

    1. Interpret the SMR of one county of your choice in a full sentence a county commissioner could understand.

Sullivan County had an SMR of 0.395 meaning it experienced about 60.5% fewer Covid deaths than would be expected if the county had followed the statewide mortality rate. 

b. Divide each county's crude rate by the statewide rate and compare with the
   SMR. Explain why they are identical here, and what $E_i$ would have to
   take into account for the two to differ. *(This is where we are going
   later in the semester.)*

Dividing each county’s crude mortality rate by the statewide mortality rate produces the same value as the SMR because the expected count was calculated using only the statewide rate and county population. The two measures would differ if the expected counts were adjusted for other factors, such as differences in age structure or other demographic characteristics across counties.

  1. Compute an exact 95% confidence interval for every SMR (formula below). Compare the intervals for the two or three counties with the fewest deaths with those of the counties with the highest SMRs. In three or four sentences: what does this tell you about the extreme values on an SMR map?

The counties with the fewest deaths have much wider confidence intervals than counties with larger numbers of deaths. For example, Sullivan County had an SMR of .39, but its 95% confidence interval ranged from .08 to 1.15, indicating substantial uncertainty. Several of the low death counties also have confidence intervals that include 1, suggesting their mortality experience may not be really different from the statewide average. This shows that extreme values on an SMR map, especially in counties with small numbers of deaths, can be unstable and should be interpreted carefully.

NoteWhere the confidence interval comes from

Treat the expected count \(E\) as a fixed constant and the observed count as Poisson, \(O \sim \text{Poisson}(\mu)\) with \(\mu = \text{SMR} \times E\). We first find an exact 95% interval for \(\mu\) and then divide both ends by \(E\).

The lower bound \(\mu_L\) is the value of \(\mu\) at which observing \(O\) or more deaths has probability 0.025; the upper bound \(\mu_U\) is the value at which observing \(O\) or fewer has probability 0.025. Because of the link between the Poisson and chi-square distributions, both have a closed form:

\[ \mu_L = \tfrac{1}{2}\,\chi^2_{0.025,\;2O}, \qquad \mu_U = \tfrac{1}{2}\,\chi^2_{0.975,\;2(O+1)} . \]

Dividing by \(E\) gives the interval for the SMR:

\[ \left[\ \frac{\chi^2_{0.025,\,2O}}{2E}\ ,\ \ \frac{\chi^2_{0.975,\,2(O+1)}}{2E}\ \right]. \]

The upper bound uses \(2(O+1)\) degrees of freedom and the lower bound \(2O\); that asymmetry is what keeps the interval exact when counts are small. When \(O = 0\) the lower bound is 0.

Worked example. A county with \(O = 4\) and \(E = 5.57\) has SMR \(= 0.72\) and

qchisq(0.025, 2 * 4)       / (2 * 5.57)   # 0.20
qchisq(0.975, 2 * (4 + 1)) / (2 * 5.57)   # 1.84
poisson.test(4, T = 5.57)$conf.int        # same interval: E acts as the "time base"

The familiar normal approximation, \(\text{SMR} \times \exp(\pm 1.96/\sqrt{O})\), works for counties with many deaths but breaks down for the smallest ones — which are exactly the counties this question is about — and is undefined when \(O = 0\).

pa_covid <- pa_covid |>
  mutate(SMR_lo = qchisq(0.025, 2 * deaths_2020) / (2 * E),

Part D — Mapping a ratio (3.5 points)

In Exercise 1 a sequential palette was the right choice for a rate. An SMR is different: it is a ratio with a meaningful reference value of 1, and it is multiplicative — an SMR of 2 is as far above expected as 0.5 is below it.

  1. Map the SMR as an interactive leaflet map with a diverging palette centred on 1 and class breaks you set yourself. Choose breaks that are symmetric on the ratio scale, and make the class around 1 read as “about as expected”. Justify the palette and the breaks in three or four sentences.

    I used a diverging RdBu color palette because an SMR of 1 represents the expected value. The class breaks are symmetric around on the ratio scale so values above or below 1 are treated equally. .8 to 1.25 represents counties with mortality close to expected. The colors make it easy to see areas with lower than expected and higher than expected mortality.

  2. Your SMR map meets the standards from Exercise 1 — legend title with units or meaning, thin boundaries, colour-blind-safe palette — and in addition:

    • a source line on the map naming the data and the year;
    • a popup for each county giving the observed and expected deaths, the SMR, and its 95% interval from C5. This is what makes an interactive map worth having: the reader can check how much evidence stands behind a colour.
Warningleaflet wants longitude and latitude

Web maps are drawn on a Web Mercator basemap and expect coordinates in EPSG:4326. Your pa_covid is now projected (Part B), so give leaflet a transformed copy, st_transform(pa_covid, 4326), and keep the projected object for everything else. Handing it projected coordinates is the most common reason for a blank leaflet map.

TipWhat earns full marks here

Breaks that follow from what an SMR means, not from the distribution of the values. A student who can explain why 0.67 and 1.5 belong in the same break set understands the variable.

Starting code

pa_wgs <- st_transform(pa_covid, 4326)      # leaflet needs lon/lat

# D1 -- breaks symmetric on the ratio scale: 1/x and x
brks <- c(0, .5, .67, .8, 1.25, 1.5, 2, Inf)

pal <- colorBin("RdBu", domain = pa_wgs$SMR, bins = brks,
                reverse = TRUE)             # red = high

leaflet(pa_wgs) |>
  addTiles() |>                               # OpenStreetMap basemap
  addPolygons(
    fillColor = ~pal(SMR), fillOpacity = 0.8,
    color = "white", weight = 0.6,          # thin boundaries
    label = ~NAME,                          # shown on hover
    popup = ~sprintf("<b>%s County</b><br>Observed: %d<br>Expected: %.1f<br>SMR: %.2f (95%% CI %.2f-%.2f)",
                     NAME, deaths_2020, E, SMR, SMR_lo, SMR_hi),
    highlightOptions = highlightOptions(weight = 2, color = "black",
                                        bringToFront = TRUE)
  ) |>
  addLegend(pal = pal, values = ~SMR, opacity = 0.8,
            title = "SMR", labFormat = labelFormat(digits = 2)) |>
  addControl("Source: PA Covid Deaths 2020", position = "bottomleft")   # source line
Note

A leaflet map is an HTML widget: it appears in the rendered page on your GitHub Pages site, which is where I grade it. It will not appear in a PDF.

Part E — Spatial weights and global Moran’s I (4 points)

  1. Build a queen contiguity neighbour list. Report the average number of neighbours, the smallest and largest, and whether any county has none.

    The queen contingency neighbor list contains 67 counties and 342 nonzero links. Counties have an average of 5.10 neighbors, the smallest number of neighbors was 2, and the largest 9. No. ounties have zero neighbors since the least connected counties each have two neighboring counties.

  2. Convert it to row-standardized spatial weights. One sentence: what does row standardization do to a county’s neighbours, and what does the spatial lag of the SMR then represent?

    Row standardization scales the weights for each county so that the weights assigned to its neighbors sum to 1 and the spatial lag of the SMR represents the weighted average SMR for neighboring counties.

  3. Compute global Moran’s I for the SMR by permutation with moran.mc() (999 simulations; set a seed), and plot the permutation distribution with the observed value marked. Report \(I\), its expectation under the null hypothesis, \(-1/(n-1)\), and the \(p\)-value. In three or four sentences: what exactly is the null hypothesis, how does the simulation test it, and is there a spatial signal in the SMRs?

    Morgan’s I was .289 compared with an expected value of -.015 under the null hypothesis.

  4. Draw the Moran scatterplot, with every county labelled and coloured by quadrant. Name two or three counties in the high–high quadrant and two or three in the low–low quadrant, say in one sentence what the slope of the fitted line is, and say in one sentence what Moran’s I does not tell you about these counties.

    Counties that are in the high high quadrant are Mifflin and Northumberland counties, while the low low quadrant are Greene and Forest counties. The upward slope of the fitted line shows that counties with high SMRs tend to be near other counties with high SMRs and those with low tend to be near other countiues with low SMRs as well. Morgan’s I does not tell us why these patterns exist, but only that similar values tend to cluster together in space.

Starting code

# E1
nb <- poly2nb(pa_covid, queen = TRUE)
summary(nb)
Neighbour list object:
Number of regions: 67 
Number of nonzero links: 342 
Percentage nonzero weights: 7.618623 
Average number of links: 5.104478 
Link number distribution:

 2  3  4  5  6  7  8  9 
 3  7 14 18 15  3  5  2 
3 least connected regions:
7 21 52 with 2 links
2 most connected regions:
4 67 with 9 links
# E2
lw <- nb2listw(nb, style = "W")

# E3 -- shuffle the SMRs across counties 999 times
set.seed(374)
mc <- moran.mc(pa_covid$SMR, lw, nsim = 999)
mc

    Monte-Carlo simulation of Moran I

data:  pa_covid$SMR 
weights: lw  
number of simulations + 1: 1000 

statistic = 0.28933, observed rank = 1000, p-value = 0.001
alternative hypothesis: greater
-1 / (nrow(pa_covid) - 1)          # expectation under the null
[1] -0.01515152
hist(mc$res, breaks = 40, main = "Permutation distribution of I", xlab = "I")
abline(v = mc$statistic, col = "red", lwd = 2)
# E4 -- moran.plot() labels only influential points; build it in ggplot2
mp_df <- pa_covid |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  mutate(lag_SMR = lag.listw(lw, SMR),          # mean SMR of neighbours
         quad = case_when(
           SMR >= mean(SMR) & lag_SMR >= mean(SMR) ~ "High-High",
           SMR <  mean(SMR) & lag_SMR <  mean(SMR) ~ "Low-Low",
           SMR >= mean(SMR) & lag_SMR <  mean(SMR) ~ "High-Low",
           TRUE                                    ~ "Low-High"))

ggplot(mp_df, aes(SMR, lag_SMR)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(mp_df$SMR), linetype = 2, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(mp_df$SMR), linetype = 2, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = quad), size = 2) +
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = NAME), size = 2.6, max.overlaps = Inf) +   # every county
  labs(x = "SMR", y = "Spatial lag of SMR", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
table(mp_df$quad)

High-High  High-Low  Low-High   Low-Low 
       21         9        13        24

Rubric

Part What is assessed Points
A Mismatched rows found and explained; key built as text; join verified with code; left vs inner join explained 3
B Correct projected CRS, stated and justified 1.5

D Diverging leaflet map centred on 1 with defended breaks; standards, source line and popup 3.5
E Weights built and described; Moran’s I by permutation, null hypothesis stated and interpreted; scatterplot read 4

Writing counts for roughly 10% of the mark within each part. A submission that is all code and no sentences cannot score above about 60%.
